job: Fresh graduate in business, finance and accounting
name: Colin Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at nine in a co-working space in Bristol where my fintech startup rents a floor. I'm a junior analyst on the payments team, so I match transactions between our platform and the banks and chase the breaks. Half my morning is writing little scripts with an AI assistant to do the matching, and the afternoon is calls with the support team about the odd cases. I live with two flatmates in Bedminster and cook for all three of us on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get into that job?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did finance and management at a university in the south-west, with a good result, and one internship at a small bank where I kept automating the boring spreadsheets. My manager noticed, and that was the interview. My dad is a bricklayer and my mum works in a school kitchen, so they're proud but a bit lost about what I actually do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say it's useful but overhyped, and I'd say that while using it all day. Online I'd probably post that people expected a revolution and got a better autocomplete. I'd tell friends that the real changes are in who owns the tools, not in the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means my plan just works. I'm good with the tools, my firm is growing, and a plateau gives me more time to climb. I'd get a promotion in about two years if the startup survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and build more of the matching scripts so I'm the one who owns the process. I'd put 250 a month into a savings account and take one of the evening courses on payments systems. I'd also keep up the Sunday cooking and the five-a-side with my flatmates, because that stuff matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. It's nice to picture a world where my skills stay valuable and I'm not racing against the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if the startup survives. How safe is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not very. It raised money 14 months ago and the runway is about a year and a half. Startups die for boring reasons, and I'd have to find another job quickly, though payments skills travel well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it went under next spring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the three people I know at the banks and a recruiter I met last month. I'd also freelance for a few weeks, building reconciliation scripts for small shops, since two of them already asked me.

say: I'd say AI is useful but **overhyped**, while using it all day.
I'd say the real fight is who **owns** the tools.
think: My plan just works: skills in demand and a firm that's **growing**.
The real risk is the startup running out of **runway**, not AI.
do: Build more matching **scripts** so I own the process.
Put **250 a month** into savings and take an evening payments course.
Keep the freelance **contacts** warm in case the startup fails.
feel: Pretty **calm**, since my skills stay valuable and there's no race.
S0.quote: Startups die for boring reasons, and I'd have to find another job quickly, though payments skills travel well.
fieldNote: Colin's calm comes from **skills** that travel, not from job security.
His one honest risk is the startup's runway.
He already has freelance interest from two small shops.

steps.text: Write more matching scripts so I own the reconciliation process
Put 250 a month into a savings account
Take the evening course on payments systems
Carry on with the payments team and push for a promotion

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is the moment to get ahead of it. I'd run a lunch session showing the team how I use the assistant, and I'd ask our boss for a clear policy on what's automated. Online I'd argue that the gains should be shared with the people who do the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think the entry-level layer is shrinking and I'm lucky to be in early. The firm would hire fewer juniors, and the ones who stay would manage the tools. I'd be fine, but the graduate behind me might not be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put up a proper tool that does 80 percent of my matching, then ask to move up to owning the exceptions. I'd start freelancing evenings for small shops, about 300 a month, as a second source of income. I'd also join the tech workers' branch of the union, since someone needs to ask for training and fairness.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anxious. My own job looks safe, but the friends who didn't learn the tools look much less safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said friends are less safe. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My flatmate Dev, who graduated in marketing and does content briefs. He refuses to use the tools because he thinks it's cheating. I've shown him twice, and I'm worried he'll get cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your union branch ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Training paid for by the firm, notice before a role is automated and some share of the savings. It's not extreme, it's how a decent workplace works.

say: I'd say this is the moment to **get ahead** of it and run a lunch session.
I'd argue gains should be **shared** with the people who do the work.
think: The **entry-level** layer is shrinking and I'm lucky to be in early.
My job looks safe, but the **graduate** behind me might not be.
do: Build a tool that handles **80 percent** of my matching and own the exceptions.
Start **freelancing** evenings for small shops, about 300 a month.
Join the tech workers' **union** branch and ask for paid training.
feel: **Uneasy**, because my job looks safe but friends who skipped the tools do not.
S1.quote: My own job looks safe, but the friends who didn't learn the tools look much less safe.
fieldNote: Colin is **ahead** of the curve and knows it, which gives him a sense of duty.
His worry is for peers like his flatmate Dev, who refuses to use the tools.
He wants fairness written down: training, notice and shared savings.

steps.text: Build a tool that handles most of my matching work
Take freelance reconciliation jobs from small shops in the evenings
Join the tech workers' union branch and ask for paid training
Run a lunch session showing the team my assistant workflow

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we have to move fast, and I'd ask the boss for a plan for every role. Online I'd push for emergency measures, retraining wages and a share of the profits for the workers. And I'd say clearly that two years is not enough for anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job as it is gets automated by 2028, and so does most of the team's. I'd have a better chance than most because I know how the tools work, but there are only so many places for a person who orchestrates them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pile on savings, about 700 a month, and cut the extras. I'd pitch the startup to let me move into the role of running the automated process, and at the same time I'd put the freelance work into a small business, so I'm not tied to one employer. I'd also ask my parents if my brother Felix, who's an apprentice electrician, could keep going with his, since hands-on trades have three more years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and a bit excited, which is weird. I don't love the pace, and I'd be furious if nobody planned for the people who can't adapt as I can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said excited. What part?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The part where I get to build something myself. The tools make a one-person firm possible, but it's a selfish excitement, and I'd feel bad saying it to my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you protect your parents in this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mum's school kitchen job and Dad's bricklaying are hands-on, so the first shock doesn't hit them. But their pension fund and the prices at the shop would feel it. I'd help them move savings into something safer and I'd offer to pay for a few bills.

say: I'd ask the boss for a **plan** for every role.
I'd push for retraining wages and a **profit share** for workers.
think: My job as it is gets **automated** by 2028, along with most of the team's.
I'd have a **better chance** than most because I know the tools.
do: Save about **700 a month** and cut the extras.

Turn the freelance work into a small **business** so I'm not tied to one employer.
feel: **Anxious** and a bit excited, but furious if no one plans for people who can't adapt.
S2.quote: The tools make a one-person firm possible, but it's a selfish excitement, and I'd feel bad saying it to my mum.
fieldNote: Colin is **anxious** but sees an opening, and he is honest about the guilt in that.
He puts his hands-on family as buffer, not as a worry for now.
He has a concrete plan: running the process or going solo.

steps.text: Save about 700 a month into a high-interest account
Cancel streaming and takeaways and cut the gym
Pitch the startup for the job of running the automated payments process
Register the freelance reconciliation work as a small business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a good run-up, as long as people use it. At work I'd offer to teach the team, and online I'd talk about how to share the gains, like worker shares or a basic income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm fairly calm. In five years I'd be 27 with a track record, a few contacts and probably a small business on the side. The risk is that the shift is faster than the safety nets, which is what governments always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the freelance work to about 600 a month, then decide whether to go full time. I'd save towards a deposit anyway, about 400 a month, but keep it flexible. I'd also teach my dad and my brother to use the tools for their own quotes and invoices, so they're not left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but optimistic. I like having time, and I think I'd enjoy the tinkering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd teach your dad. How does that go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Funny, probably. My dad still writes quotes on the back of a delivery slip, but if a tool writes the quote and the invoice in two minutes, he'd come round fast. He'd save hours a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What stops this plan from working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the tools get so good that anyone can do what I sell. Then I'm not special, and I'm competing with a thousand other one-person firms. I'd have to find the thing people still want from a person.

say: I'd say five years is a good **run-up** if people use it.
I'd offer to **teach** the team and talk up sharing gains.
think: I'm fairly calm, since I'd be **27** with a record and a side business.
The risk is the shift moving faster than the **safety nets**.

Save **400 a month** towards a deposit, kept flexible.
Teach my **dad** and brother to use the tools for quotes and invoices.
feel: **Uneasy** but optimistic, since time makes the tinkering enjoyable.
S3.quote: My dad still writes quotes on the back of a delivery slip, but if a tool writes the quote and the invoice in two minutes, he'd come round fast.
fieldNote: Colin sees five years as time to **build** a business and bring family along.

steps.text: Grow freelance reconciliation work to about 600 a month
Save 400 a month towards a flexible house deposit
Show Dad how a tool writes quotes and invoices
Help my brother Felix plan his apprenticeship years

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time to have this go well, if we agree rules now. At work I'd keep showing people the tools, and online I'd go on about fair shares and public training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel good about this. By 2036 I'd be 32, with a company or a senior role, and a decade of knowing how the tools work. I'd probably be the person helping others through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep building and slowly turn the freelance work into a proper small firm with one or two staff, who I'd pay fairly. I'd also put money into an index fund each month, about 300, and maybe buy a flat. And I'd give some time to a training charity helping adults retrain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit proud. It's the world where learning early paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd pay your staff fairly. What does fair mean to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A living wage, training time and a share of the profit once the firm is stable. If I'm making money because a machine makes my team more productive, they should see it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this world that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the gains went to a handful of firms and the rest of us got nothing. Ten years lets me argue and vote about it, but I've seen how slowly politics moves.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty** if we agree the rules now.
I'd keep showing people the **tools** and talk up fair shares.
think: I feel good, because by 2036 I'd be **32** with a decade of tool skills.
I'd probably be the person **helping** others through it.
do: Turn the freelance work into a small **firm** with one or two paid staff.
Put **300 a month** into an index fund and maybe buy a flat.

feel: **Calm** and a bit proud, since learning early paid off.
S4.quote: If I'm making money because a machine makes my team more productive, they should see it.
fieldNote: Colin's **optimism** is tied to his own readiness and a sense of fairness.
He imagines himself as employer and guide, not only as survivor.
Still worried about the gains going to a few firms.

steps.text: Turn the freelance work into a small firm with two paid staff
Put 300 a month into an index fund

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, though I'd be more ready than most. What would help is a proper retraining wage and a rule that gains from automation are shared, like through worker shares. I'd also want my brother Felix and my parents covered, because I'm the one who can adapt and they're not.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether I feel guilty. I use the tools every day and I know I'm making some jobs smaller, so the people who gain should pay for the people who lose. I don't think the answer is to stop.

headlineQuote: I use the tools every day and I know I'm making some jobs smaller, so the people who gain should pay for the people who lose.
portrait: Colin, 22, is a **junior analyst** on the payments team of a Bristol fintech startup.
He uses AI tools **every day**, builds scripts and already has freelance clients on the side.
Progressive and adaptive, he wants **shared gains**, union training and rules rather than a stop to the technology.
He moves from calm to **anxious** at two years, but always has a build-something plan.
His parents' hands-on jobs and his brother's electrical apprenticeship ground his choices.
biggestWorry: The **2028** world, mostly for people who cannot adapt as he can, such as his parents and friends.
whatWouldHelp: A retraining **wage** and a rule that gains from automation are shared with workers.
